tldr: The paper introduces CycleResearcher and CycleReviewer, an iterative preference training framework using open-source LLMs to automate the full research-review-refinement cycle, achieving competitive simulated peer review scores and improved review prediction accuracy.
contributions: Two large-scale datasets: Review-5k (4,991 papers from ICLR 2024 with 16,000+ reviewer comments) and Research-14k (12,696 training samples of accepted ML papers from 2022-2024)
An iterative SimPO training framework with CycleResearcher (policy model) and CycleReviewer (reward model) ranging from 12B to 123B parameters
Demonstration that CycleReviewer reduces MAE by 26.89% compared to individual human reviewers
Evidence that CycleResearcher-generated papers achieve simulated peer review scores of 5.36, approaching the human preprint level of 5.24 and accepted paper level of 5.69
methods: The authors train two open-source LLMs (based on Mistral and Qwen 2.5, 12B-123B) using an iterative Simple Preference Optimization (SimPO) framework. CycleResearcher simulates literature review, hypothesis formulation, experimental design, and paper writing (with fabricated experimental results to accelerate training). CycleReviewer simulates peer review by generating feedback and scores (1-10 scale) across multiple dimensions. In each iteration, CycleResearcher generates papers, CycleReviewer evaluates them, and pairwise preference data (highest vs. lowest scored papers) is used to update the policy model via SimPO combined with negative log-likelihood loss. Training used 8x H100 GPUs with learning rates of 1e-5 (reviewer) and 4e-5 (researcher).
results: CycleReviewer achieved a 26.89% reduction in mean absolute error (MAE) compared to individual human reviewers on the Review-5k test set. Papers generated by CycleResearcher scored 5.36 in simulated peer reviews, compared to 5.24 for human preprints and 5.69 for accepted papers. The model achieved an acceptance rate of 31.07% in simulated reviews. Models were evaluated using proxy MAE/MSE with independent unbiased estimators as ground truth surrogates.
limitations: The framework uses fabricated experimental results rather than actual experiments, limiting real-world validity. Generalizability across research domains remains a challenge for current LLMs. The generated papers still score below the accepted paper level (5.36 vs 5.69), indicating room for improvement. Memory constraints require truncation of samples exceeding context length. The approach focuses on ideation and writing, excluding actual experiment execution.
